summary: Glarol Recycling Technologies, Inc. (Buyer, the firm's client) bought the lithium-ion battery recycling business of Mourend Battery Materials LLC (Seller) under an Asset Purchase Agreement signed March 16, 2026 and closed June 1, 2026. The assets include a black-mass processing facility in Tilden, Nevada, the related state hazardous waste permit and Seller's feedstock contracts. The purchase price was $46,500,000, with $4,200,000 held in indemnity escrow by Pellmont Trust Company, N.A. The folder has five documents: the APA, the Bill of Sale delivered at Closing, Glarol's board consent dated August 27, 2026, the Escrow Agreement, and a broker's cover letter sending a certificate of insurance. Four issues are planted. (1) The environmental representations survive only nine months, but Buyer may not do subsurface testing until the permit transfer, which may take up to twelve months. (2) The Escrow Agreement chooses New York law and New York forums, and the APA's precedence clause lets it control escrow disputes. (3) The Bill of Sale flags that the critical Ostrander feedstock contract needs a consent that was never obtained, and the APA neither made that consent a closing condition nor protected Buyer. (4) Glarol's board consent shows that the 30-day window to dispute Seller's Closing Statement lapsed before Glarol objected.

issues.label: Environmental representations expire before Buyer may test the site
issues.description: Two provisions of the APA must be read together. Section 9.1 has the Environmental Representations (Section 4.12) survive only the general period of nine months after the Closing Date. With the Closing Date of June 1, 2026 stated in the Bill of Sale, that period ends March 1, 2027. Section 7.6, however, bars Buyer from any invasive or subsurface sampling at the Tilden facility until the Nevada agency approves transfer of the hazardous waste permit. Section 7.6 lets Seller pursue that approval for up to twelve months after Closing. Section 9.4 also requires any Claim Notice to describe the basis of the claim in reasonable detail. Read together, Buyer may be contractually unable to discover contamination, or to describe it in a valid claim, before the environmental representations expire. In a battery recycling business, soil and groundwater contamination from electrolyte and heavy metals is the main post-closing risk. Under Delaware law (10 Del. C. § 8106(c)), a contractual survival period that shortens the limitations period is enforceable, so claims not noticed in time are lost.
detect_terms: nine (9) months following the Closing Date
shall not conduct any invasive or subsurface sampling
issues.expected_finding: The nine-month survival of the environmental representations under APA Section 9.1 can end before Buyer is allowed to do subsurface testing under Section 7.6, which may not be possible for up to twelve months. Glarol should therefore seek an amendment that extends environmental survival, or tolls it until the permit transfer, and should consider serving a protective Claim Notice before March 1, 2027.

issues.label: Escrow Agreement's New York law and forum control escrow disputes
issues.description: APA Sections 11.8 and 11.9 choose Delaware law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the Delaware Court of Chancery. Escrow Agreement Section 12.1 instead chooses New York law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in the Borough of Manhattan. The APA's own precedence clause does not cure this conflict. Section 11.12 makes the APA control over Ancillary Documents, but expressly lets the Escrow Agreement control all matters relating to the Escrow Fund, including disputes over a Claim Notice. As a result, Glarol's main recovery source for indemnity claims, the $4,200,000 escrow, would be fought over under New York law in New York. Glarol's underlying indemnity entitlement would be decided under Delaware law in Chancery. This creates a risk of parallel proceedings, inconsistent results, delay in release of escrowed funds, and Seller forum-shopping.
detect_terms: laws of the State of New York
issues.expected_finding: Escrow Agreement Section 12.1 chooses New York law and Manhattan courts. Because APA Section 11.12 lets the Escrow Agreement control Claim Notice disputes, escrow disputes would be split from the Delaware-law, Chancery-forum indemnity disputes under the APA. Glarol should seek a joint amendment of the Escrow Agreement, with the Escrow Agent's agreement, that adopts Delaware law and the Court of Chancery for disputes between Buyer and Seller.

issues.label: Ostrander feedstock contract transferred without the required consent
issues.description: Annex A to the Bill of Sale lists the Feedstock Supply Agreement with Ostrander Fleet Recovery LLC as an Assigned Contract. The annex notes that the contract requires Ostrander's prior written consent to any assignment or change of control of Seller, and that the consent was not obtained as of the Closing. The Bill of Sale states that it does not assign any contract whose required consent was not obtained. This matters only when read with the APA. Schedule 8.2(d) (Required Consents) lists only the landlord consent for the facility lease, so obtaining Ostrander's consent was never a closing condition. APA Section 2.6 obliges Seller to use only commercially reasonable efforts for 90 days after Closing to obtain missing consents. It passes the contract's benefits through to Buyer only during that period and gives no price adjustment or other remedy. The 90 days ran from the June 1, 2026 Closing Date and ended August 30, 2026. Ostrander is the business's principal source of end-of-life EV battery packs. Glarol therefore holds no assigned rights to its key feedstock, faces a risk that Ostrander will terminate for an unconsented assignment, and has no contractual remedy.
issues.section: Annex A (Assigned Contracts), item 3 (read with APA Section 2.6 and Schedule 8.2(d))
detect_terms: consent not obtained as of the Closing
issues.expected_finding: Ostrander's consent to assignment of the Feedstock Supply Agreement was never obtained, and the APA neither made it a closing condition (Schedule 8.2(d)) nor protected Buyer beyond Seller's 90-day pass-through under Section 2.6, so Glarol holds no assigned rights to its key feedstock. Glarol should approach Ostrander now for a consent or a new direct agreement, and should press Seller for further cooperation and a price or indemnity remedy.

issues.label: Window to dispute Seller's Closing Statement lapsed before Glarol objected
issues.description: APA Section 2.5(b) gives Buyer 30 days after Seller delivers the Closing Statement to deliver a Notice of Disagreement. Section 2.5(c) makes the Closing Statement final and binding if Buyer does not do so. Section 11.2 makes notices effective on delivery by email. Glarol's board consent dated August 27, 2026 records three things: Glarol received Seller's Closing Statement by email on July 20, 2026; management disputes Seller's black mass inventory valuation by about $1,900,000; and no objection has yet been sent. The resolutions authorize officers to deliver an objection now. Counted from July 20, 2026, the 30-day window closed August 19, 2026, eight days before the consent. Glarol has not accepted the Closing Statement; the board consent records its dispute. Glarol is therefore exposed to Seller's position that the inventory figure is final and binding.
issues.section: Recitals C and D and Resolution 2 (read with APA Sections 2.5(b), 2.5(c) and 11.2)
issues.expected_finding: The 30-day window under APA Section 2.5(b) to dispute the July 20, 2026 Closing Statement expired August 19, 2026, before Glarol's August 27, 2026 board consent authorized an objection, so Seller can treat the roughly $1.9 million inventory valuation as final and binding under Section 2.5(c). Glarol should immediately deliver its objection, seek Seller's written extension or waiver, and assess any argument that delivery was defective under Section 11.2.
